name: Diego Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I'm not much of a talker, but go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a patrol car on the south side of the city, mostly the ring road and the industrial estates, with a fair bit of traffic work. A day is speeding stops, crashes, a stolen van now and then, and whatever the control room throws at us when it gets busy. I'm still green; I fumble the breath test paperwork and my partner, Kev, has to remind me of the steps. I carry a paper notebook as well as the tablet because I don't trust the tablet. I like the driving and the quiet stretches. I don't like the crash scenes with kids involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Suits me. I've never been sold on any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: it's a tool like any other and the job's still the job. I'm not one for posting online, so it'd be a comment in the canteen at most. Something like, so much for the robot traffic cops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm slow with the tablet already, and I was worried they'd load more onto it. If nothing really changes, I keep learning the job at my own pace. Pay's good, the flat's mine apart from a small loan, and there's always police work in a city this size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the same thing: get better at the breath test procedure and the crash reports, and keep my notebook. I'd keep saving 400 a month, same as now. Maybe in a year or two I'd go for the advanced driving course, since that's the part I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd sleep fine. It's the version I quietly expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the flat's yours apart from a small loan. How did that happen at 27?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandfather left me some money when he died. My dad told me to put my grandfather's money in bricks, not a car. Nobody can put the rent up on me. So I bought a one-bedroom near the bus depot, and it's not much, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still bothers you at work, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crash scenes. You don't get used to them, whatever people say. And the speed cameras already do half of what we used to, so the traffic team keeps getting smaller even without fancy AI.

say: I'd say it's a **tool like any other** and the job hasn't changed.
I'd make a quiet canteen joke about the **robot traffic cops** that never came.
think: I'm **slow with the tablet**, so fewer new systems suits me fine.
Good pay and a **nearly paid flat** make me feel secure.
do: Keep practising the **breath test** procedure and crash reports.
Consider the **advanced driving** course in a year or two.
S0.quote: My dad told me to put my grandfather's money in bricks, not a car. Nobody can put the rent up on me.
fieldNote: He keeps a **paper notebook** alongside the tablet out of distrust.
His security rests on a **flat bought** with his grandfather's money, which he mentions with pride.
He notes **speed cameras** already shrank traffic policing, even without AI.

steps.text: Keep practising the breath test procedure and crash reports
Apply for the advanced driving course in a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one sounds like what's creeping in anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, some of the paperwork could go to a computer. I wouldn't make a fuss in public. At most I'd tell my mates in the pub that traffic policing is going to be cameras and a couple of us left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it hits traffic harder than most. The cameras catch speeders, the computer writes the crash report, the van's tracker tells you where it is. That's my week. I'd still have a job somewhere in the force, but maybe not in a car, which is the bit I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the new training when they make me, not before. I'd keep saving and maybe pay off the last of the flat loan, about 6,000, so I've got no debts at all. If the traffic team shrank, I'd ask to move back to response rather than leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it's in the back of my mind on the quiet stretches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the training when they make you, not before. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half of what they roll out gets pulled six months later. I've seen it with two tablet updates already. Why learn something twice?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first sign that it's really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they stop replacing people on the traffic team. When somebody on the traffic team retires and nobody comes in, AI has arrived, quietly, with no big announcement.

say: I'd say **fair enough** to handing some paperwork to computers.
I'd tell pub friends traffic policing will be **cameras** and a few officers.
think: Traffic work is **hit harder**, with cameras, trackers and auto-written crash reports.
I'd likely keep a force job, but maybe not **in a car**.
do: Pay off the last **6,000 on the flat** loan.
Ask to move back to **response** if the traffic team shrinks.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, with the worry surfacing on quiet stretches of road.
S1.quote: When somebody on the traffic team retires and nobody comes in, AI has arrived, quietly, with no big announcement.
fieldNote: His resistance comes from **experience** of tools being pulled after rollout, not stubbornness alone.
He predicts **quiet attrition**, with retirements not replaced, rather than cuts.
Losing the **driving** he enjoys bothers him more than losing a job.

steps.text: Do the new reporting training only once it's required
Pay off the last 6,000 on the flat loan
Ask to move back to response if the traffic team shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, well, we'll see, out loud. I don't go on about things. If people at work were angry I'd nod along, but I wouldn't be the one leading anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be out. Traffic is the most automatic bit of policing there is, and a slow junior who won't touch the tablet is the obvious one to cut when the thinking work goes in 2028. By 2031 the robots can do the stops too. I'd have no idea what to do instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big straight away, no new car, no holiday. I'd keep every penny in savings, which is about ten months of pay. I'd ring my uncle, who runs a car body shop on the east side, and ask if he'd take me on if it came to it. I'd hate it, but at least the dents are hands-on for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the floor's gone. I'd be lying awake running numbers, and I'm not usually a worrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra three years before robots help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It means the stopping and the crash scenes still need a person till 2031. But they'd need fewer of us, because the computer does all the planning and the reports. I'd be hanging on by my fingernails for three years, until the robots can do the traffic stops too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate the body shop. Why go there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's family, and I know Uncle Marc would say yes without asking questions. I don't want to learn some new computer job at 29. Knocking dents out of wings is something I could pick up.

say: I'd say **we'll see** in public and keep my head down.
I'd **nod along** with angry colleagues but never lead anything.
think: Traffic is the **most automatic** part of policing, so I'd likely be cut.
With robots by **2031**, I'd have no idea what to do instead.
do: Stop all **big spending**, like a new car or a holiday.
Keep about **ten months' pay** in savings untouched.
Ask my **uncle's body shop** to take me on if needed.
feel: He feels the **floor has gone**, lying awake running numbers.
S2.quote: I'd be hanging on by my fingernails for three years, until the robots can do the traffic stops too.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** and admits he has no plan of his own.
He'd fall back on **family** rather than learn a new digital role.
His quiet manner hides a sharp **alarm** he rarely voices.

steps.text: Cancel the new car and the holiday this year
Keep ten months of pay in savings untouched
Ask his uncle's body shop to take him on if cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Not good, but better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd keep quiet mostly. I might say to Kev that we'd better start thinking about it. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd have more experience and maybe the advanced driving ticket. That helps a bit. But the thinking side still goes in 2031, and traffic is still first in line. I'd probably try to get onto a response team before then, where there's more people stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the advanced driving course in the first year and then ask for a move to response in year two. I'd clear the flat loan. And I'd keep an eye out, wait and see what the force does with traffic before deciding anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not like the two-year one. More like a background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kev if he asked what you're planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Kev that I'm getting off traffic before traffic gets off us. He'd laugh. He's got twenty years in, so he'll probably just make it to his pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put self-driving cars on the ring road, honestly. Fewer crashes, fewer speeders, less for us to do. That's when I'd know.

say: I'd tell my partner Kev we'd better **start thinking** about the change.
think: Five years brings **more experience** and maybe an advanced driving ticket.
Traffic is still **first in line** when thinking work goes in 2031.
do: Take the **advanced driving** course in the first year.
Ask for a move to **response** in year two.
**Wait and see** what the force does with traffic before bigger moves.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but as a background hum rather than dread.
S3.quote: I'd tell my partner Kev that I'm getting off traffic before traffic gets off us.
fieldNote: He'd act sooner if **self-driving cars** reached the ring road, a concrete trigger.
He envies his partner's **pension** timing without resentment.
More time lets him plan a **sideways move**, but not a new career.

steps.text: Take the advanced driving course in the first year
Ask for a transfer from traffic to response in year two
Watch for self-driving cars on the ring road before deciding more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be nearly 40 before robots. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's ages away and there's no point panicking. That's what I'd say at work, anyway. I'm not one for big talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough that I'd be a proper officer by then, not a junior. I'd have a decade in, the flat paid off, savings piled up. If the robots come at 40, I could switch to something then. I just don't love the thought of starting again at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and stay on traffic for a while, because I like it. I'd pay off the flat. Around year five I'd look at what's left and move to response or custody if traffic's shrinking. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not worried day to day, but I know it's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the AI tools in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once they're settled and everyone uses them, yes. Not early. I'd learn the one I have to learn, properly, once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you picture yourself doing at 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a custody sergeant, booking people in, if humans still do that. Or the body shop. I can't picture myself at 40, honestly, and I'm not going to pretend I can.

say: I'd say it's **ages away** and not worth panicking about.
I'd keep **big talk** out of it at work.
think: A decade makes me a **proper officer** with the flat paid off.
Starting again **at 40** is the part I don't love.
do: Stay on **traffic** for now, because I enjoy it.
Move to response or **custody** around year five if traffic shrinks.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, aware of the change but not worried day to day.
S4.quote: I can't picture myself at 40, honestly, and I'm not going to pretend I can.
fieldNote: He'd learn AI tools **once, when settled**, a consistent thread across scenarios.
He's honest that he **can't picture** himself at 40.
Ten years gives his **resistant** style enough room to cope.

steps.text: Stay on the traffic team while it still exists
Move to response or custody around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. That's the only one where I'd actually be scared. What would help is the force moving people sideways inside policing instead of letting them go, and some kind of pay guarantee while you move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. If I lost the job, my family's the first place I'd turn, not the government. My uncle's shop, my dad's advice. I think a lot of people are like that.

headlineQuote: If I lost the job, my family's the first place I'd turn, not the government.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** traffic patrol officer who still carries a paper notebook.
He's **pragmatic** and quiet, avoiding politics and new technology until forced.
A **flat** bought with his grandfather's inheritance gives him real security.
He sees **traffic policing** as the most automatable part of the job and fears being cut.
In the **two-year** world he has no plan beyond his uncle's body shop; more time lets him move sideways.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, the only one where he'd actually be scared.
whatWouldHelp: Moving officers **sideways** inside policing rather than letting them go.
